title: Centre of gravity and the moment of a force
prior_knowledge_summary: Forces have magnitude, direction and a line of action.
Weight is the gravitational force on an object and can be calculated from mass and gravitational field strength.
SI units and simple right-angle geometry can be used in force calculations.
new_learning: Represent distributed weight as one force acting at the centre of gravity.
Define and calculate the moment of one force using its perpendicular distance from a chosen point.

visual_planning.reason: Six different sketches make distributed weight, line of action, perpendicular distance, direction and angled geometry visible without introducing equilibrium.
visual_planning.style: rectangular white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch

blocks.title: Why does a broom balance away from its middle?
content: Place one finger under the middle of a broom. It usually tips toward the heavy brush. Slide your finger toward the brush and there is one position where the broom can rest without immediately turning.

The broom has weight throughout its wood and brush. Why can one special point tell us how all of that distributed weight turns the broom? Predict where that point lies compared with the geometric middle.

figure.purpose: Create the opening prediction about an uneven mass distribution
figure.brief: Show a side view of a broom in two panels. In the first panel a finger supports the geometric middle and the brush end tips down. In the second panel the support is nearer the brush and the broom rests. Use only short labels such as middle and balance point.
figure.alt_text: A broom tips when supported at its middle but rests when supported nearer its heavy brush.

blocks.title: Replace distributed weight by one equivalent force
content: Gravity pulls on every small part of an object. Drawing thousands of tiny weight arrows would hide the useful physics. For motion and turning calculations, we replace them by one equivalent weight force.
The formal definition to remember is: the centre of gravity is the point through which the whole weight of a body may be considered to act.

The single weight arrow is drawn vertically downward through that point. The centre of gravity is a point in our model. It does not have to be a marked point on the surface, and for a hollow object it may lie in empty space.

controlled_definition.accepted_definition: the point through which the whole weight of a body may be considered to act

figure.purpose: Show the modelling step from distributed weight to one resultant weight
figure.brief: Draw an irregular object first with several small downward gravity arrows spread through it, then the same object with one downward arrow W through a labelled centre of gravity. Use a simple replacement arrow between the panels.
figure.alt_text: Many small downward gravity arrows are replaced by one weight arrow through the centre of gravity.

blocks.title: Shape alone does not locate the centre of gravity
content: For a uniform rectangular book, symmetry places the centre of gravity at its geometric centre. The mass is spread evenly, so neither side is favoured.

A hammer has a similar overall length but much more mass in its metal head. Its centre of gravity lies closer to the head. This is the broom idea again: the point follows the mass distribution, not simply the outline.

A useful test is to imagine supporting the object at the proposed point. If its weight acts through that support point, the weight has no sideways separation from it and so no turning effect about that point. We are not balancing several forces here. We are using one weight force to understand the chosen point.

figure.purpose: Contrast uniform and non-uniform mass distributions
figure.brief: Make a two-row comparison. Show a uniform book with its centre of gravity at the geometric centre and a hammer with its centre of gravity closer to the metal head. Include sparse mass shading and one downward W arrow for each.
figure.alt_text: A uniform book has a central centre of gravity while a hammer has one nearer its heavy head.

blocks.title: A force can have a turning effect
content: Push a door near its hinge and it is hard to turn. Apply the same force at the handle and it turns more easily. The force has not changed, but the separation between the hinge and the force's line of action has changed.
The formal definition to remember is: the moment of a force about a point is the product of the force and the perpendicular distance from the point to the line of action of the force.
The formula to remember is M = Fd_perp. Here M is the moment in N m, F is the force in N, and d_perp is the shortest perpendicular distance in m from the chosen point to the force's line of action.
A moment also has a sense. In a flat sketch, one force tends to turn the object either clockwise or anticlockwise about the chosen point. State the sense when the question asks for it.

controlled_definition.accepted_definition: the product of the force and the perpendicular distance from the point to the line of action of the force

figure.purpose: Distinguish the line of action and the perpendicular distance
figure.brief: Sketch a door seen from above with a hinge point, a force arrow at the handle, a dashed extension of the force's line of action and the shortest right-angle distance from hinge to that line. Add a small clockwise curved arrow.
figure.alt_text: A door diagram shows the force line of action and the perpendicular distance from the hinge.

blocks.title: Calculate one force's moment
content: A mechanic pushes with a force of 24 N on a horizontal spanner. The force acts downward and its line of action is 0.35 m from the centre of the nut.
The shortest route is the moment formula because the force and perpendicular distance are already known. M = Fd_perp = 24 N x 0.35 m = 8.4 N m.
The force is to the right of the nut and points downward, so it tends to turn the spanner clockwise. The complete result is a moment of 8.4 N m clockwise about the nut.
Check: 24 x 0.35 must be less than 24 x 1, so 8.4 N m has a sensible size. The unit N m also follows from force multiplied by distance.

figure.purpose: Model a complete one-force calculation with direction and units
figure.brief: Draw a horizontal spanner with nut centre marked as the point, a downward 24 N arrow at the right end, a 0.35 m horizontal perpendicular distance and an aligned three-line calculation M = Fd_perp, substitution and 8.4 N m clockwise.
figure.alt_text: A 24 N downward force on a spanner at 0.35 m gives an 8.4 N m clockwise moment.

blocks.title: Use the perpendicular distance, not the handle length
content: It feels natural to multiply by the distance from the pivot to the point where the force is applied. That works only when this distance is perpendicular to the force's line of action.

Imagine the same force applied along the length of a spanner toward the nut. The application point may be far from the nut, but the force's line of action passes through the nut. The perpendicular distance is zero, so the moment about the nut is zero.

Always draw or imagine the complete line of action first. Then drop the shortest line from the chosen point to it and mark the right angle. That line, not automatically the object's length, is d_perp.

blocks.title: Use centre of gravity and moment together
content: A non-uniform sign has mass 5.0 kg. Its centre of gravity is 0.60 m from a hinge along the sign, which is held 30 degrees above the horizontal. Find the moment of its weight about the hinge using g = 9.81 N kg^-1.
First replace the distributed weight by one downward force at the centre of gravity. The formula to remember is W = mg, so W = 5.0 kg x 9.81 N kg^-1 = 49.05 N.
The 0.60 m sloping length is not perpendicular to the vertical weight. The perpendicular distance is the horizontal separation: d_perp = 0.60 cos 30 degrees = 0.520 m.
Now M = Fd_perp = 49.05 N x 0.520 m = 25.5 N m, which is 25 N m to two significant figures. The weight acts to the right of the hinge and downward, so the sense is clockwise.
Check the geometry: the perpendicular distance must be less than 0.60 m, so the moment must be less than 49.05 x 0.60 = 29.4 N m. The result passes this independent check.

figure.purpose: Teach the combined route from mass distribution to perpendicular geometry and moment
figure.brief: Show a non-uniform sign hinged at the left and tilted 30 degrees above horizontal. Mark its centre of gravity 0.60 m along the sign, draw W vertically downward there, and show the horizontal perpendicular distance from hinge to the vertical line of action. Place the calculation in a separate annotation box.
figure.alt_text: An angled sign has weight acting at its centre of gravity and a horizontal perpendicular distance from the hinge.

blocks.title: A reliable one-force route
content: For an object's weight, locate the centre of gravity and draw one vertical downward weight arrow through it. If mass is given, calculate the force with W = mg.
Choose the stated point. Extend the force's line of action, find the perpendicular distance to it, and use M = Fd_perp. Finish with N m and, when required, clockwise or anticlockwise.
Stop after the one force's turning effect. Do not balance it against another moment yet. Couples, the principle of moments and complete equilibrium belong to later lessons.

concepts_taught: distributed weight represented by one equivalent force
clockwise and anticlockwise moment of one force
misconceptions_addressed: centre of gravity is always the geometric centre
distance to the force application point is always the moment arm
a force far from a pivot must produce a moment
skills_students_can_now_use: represent an object's distributed weight as acting at its centre of gravity
calculate weight from mass and gravitational field strength
identify the perpendicular distance to a force's line of action
calculate and state the sense of one force's moment
next_lesson_can_assume: the controlled definitions of centre of gravity and moment of a force
